correctness.rationale: The moment ratio is F(q^n)/F(1) by cancellation of the infinite products; F(1) is strictly positive. Normal convergence on compact subsets of the stated disk and analyticity past 1 justify absolute summation and termwise differences. Comparing coefficients in (1-az)F(z)=(1-bz)F(qz) gives the stated recurrence. The k=1 and k=2 multipliers are negative and all later ones positive, so the normalized difference bracket has one positive contribution, from k=1, and subtracts positive terms proportional to q^((k-1)n). Thus the most restrictive tail is n=0 for each order. R_m is strictly increasing and divergent and R_1<1 because the weights exceed one. For the operator equivalence, the signed alternating sum is diagonal on e_n and its entries are the normalized signed moment differences divided by the positive gamma_n. Equality at R_m=1 passes, and higher orders then fail. For fixed p and a, c_k/(-c_1) is comparable to epsilon*a^(k-2), with constants uniform in k and small epsilon: the j>=3 factors have positive uniform lower bounds and summable deviations from 1. Put r=floor(log_p m). The part k>=r costs O(a^r); for k=r-j below r, (1-q^k)^m<=exp(-p^j) gives a summable a^(-j) penalty. Conversely k=r+2 contributes at least (1-q)*a^r by Bernoulli's inequality. This gives two-sided m^(-beta), even when r<2 with the lower part empty. The inequalities at M and M+1 now bracket L*M-beta*log M within a bounded additive distance of log(1/epsilon); M tends to infinity since each fixed R_m tends to zero. First M is comparable to log(1/epsilon), and substituting its logarithm proves the asserted log-log term and bounded error. This does not identify a constant for the remainder or give uniformity when p or a varies.

value.rationale: The result quantifies how long finite-order tests can silently pass just outside a known all-order sector. The log-log delay is not captured by monitoring any one fixed atom and is relevant to interpreting order-limited tests. An exact criterion uniform over starting index and a two-term boundary law supply more than a qualitative failure of complete hyperexpansivity.
